questions.s: Concerning the nerves of the anterior abdominal wall:
o: The lower six thoracic nerves run between internal oblique and transversus abdominis

The lower six thoracic nerves run forward between internal oblique and transversus abdominis, the neurovascular plane of the abdominal wall.
This plane is used for transversus abdominis plane (TAP) blocks.
T10 supplies the skin of the umbilicus

T10 supplies the skin of the umbilicus. T7 supplies the subcostal angle and T8 the rib margin.
Umbilical referred pain (for example early appendicitis) is T10.
The iliohypogastric nerve pierces the external oblique aponeurosis about 2.5 cm above the superficial ring

The iliohypogastric nerve pierces the external oblique aponeurosis about 2.5 cm above the superficial ring to supply the suprapubic skin.
It can be injured in appendicectomy incisions.
The ilioinguinal nerve enters the inguinal canal through the deep ring

Last's says the ilioinguinal nerve enters the inguinal canal from the side by piercing internal oblique, not through the deep ring, and emerges through the superficial ring.
So it is not a content of the spermatic cord.

questions.s: Damage to the ilioinguinal nerve within the inguinal canal would cause:
o: Weakness of the conjoint tendon

Last's says that within the canal the ilioinguinal nerve is sensory only; its motor branch to internal oblique and transversus has already been given off.
So the conjoint tendon is not weakened.
Sensory loss over the root of the penis and anterior scrotum

The ilioinguinal nerve (L1) supplies the skin over the root of the penis and the anterior scrotum (or labium majus).
Injury in hernia repair causes numbness here.
Loss of the cremasteric reflex

The efferent limb of the cremasteric reflex is the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve, which supplies cremaster.
The ilioinguinal nerve may contribute to the afferent limb only.
Sensory loss over the upper medial thigh

The ilioinguinal nerve also supplies the skin of the upper medial thigh, below the medial end of the inguinal ligament.
Answer B: 2 and 4.

questions.s: Regarding the inguinal canal and spermatic cord:
o: The genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve is a content of the spermatic cord

The genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve is a content of the spermatic cord and supplies cremaster.
It enters the canal through the deep ring.
The ilioinguinal nerve is a content of the spermatic cord

The ilioinguinal nerve lies in the inguinal canal but outside the coverings of the spermatic cord.
It enters the canal from the side, not through the deep ring.
The lacunar ligament forms the medial margin of the femoral ring

The lacunar ligament forms the medial margin of the femoral ring, with its crescentic free edge.
This sharp edge can strangulate a femoral hernia.
The conjoint tendon is formed by internal oblique and transversus abdominis aponeuroses

The conjoint tendon is formed by the aponeuroses of internal oblique and transversus abdominis and is attached to the pubic crest and pectineal line.
It reinforces the posterior wall medially.

questions.s: Regarding the innervation of the testis:
o: It receives no parasympathetic supply

The testis receives no parasympathetic supply; the gonads and suprarenals receive only sympathetic fibres.
A favourite exam point.
Its sympathetic supply is mainly from the T10 segment

The sympathetic supply of the testis comes mainly from the T10 segment and reaches it along the testicular artery.
Testicular pain is felt around the umbilicus (T10).
Testicular pain afferents run with the testicular artery and splanchnic nerves to the T10 dorsal root ganglion

Testicular pain afferents run with the testicular artery and the splanchnic nerves to the T10 dorsal root ganglion.
Hence the referral of testicular pain to the umbilical region.
Its preganglionic sympathetic fibres relay in the coeliac ganglion region before running with the testicular artery

Last's says preganglionic fibres from about T10 reach the coeliac ganglion region (via the greater or lesser splanchnic nerves) and postganglionic fibres follow the testicular artery.
All four true: E.
It arises from the discs and the fibrous arches over the bodies of T12 to L5, and the transverse processes

Psoas major arises from the discs and the fibrous arches over the bodies of T12 to L5, and from the transverse processes. The lumbar arteries, veins and sympathetic rami pass beneath the arches.
The lumbar plexus forms within the muscle.
It is supplied by L1 to L3, mainly L2

Psoas major is supplied directly by branches of L1 to L3, mainly L2.
So it is a good test of upper lumbar roots.
Its fascia forms the medial arcuate ligament

The thickened psoas fascia forms the medial arcuate ligament, from the body of L1 (or L2) to the L1 transverse process.
The diaphragm arises from it.
Its fascia is part of the thoracolumbar (lumbar) fascia

Last's says the psoas fascia is not part of the lumbar (thoracolumbar) fascia, though its lateral edge blends with the anterior layer.
A psoas abscess tracks within its own sheath to the thigh.
Lies in the anterior compartment of the lumbar fascia

Quadratus lumborum lies in the anterior compartment of the lumbar fascia, between its anterior and middle layers. Erector spinae lies in the posterior compartment.
The fascia wraps around both muscles.
Arises from the iliolumbar ligament and iliac crest

Quadratus lumborum arises from the iliolumbar ligament, the iliac crest and the L5 transverse process.
It runs up to the twelfth rib.
Inserts into the medial half of the twelfth rib

Quadratus lumborum inserts into the medial half of the twelfth rib and the L1 to L4 transverse processes.
It fixes the twelfth rib during inspiration.
Is supplied by the obturator nerve

Quadratus lumborum is supplied by the anterior rami of T12 to L3, not by the obturator nerve.
Answer C: 1, 2 and 3.
The right trunk lies behind the inferior vena cava

The right lumbar sympathetic trunk lies behind the inferior vena cava; the left lies along the left margin of the aorta.
So the right trunk is hidden at operation.
It lies in front of the lumbar vessels

The lumbar sympathetic trunks lie in front of the lumbar vessels, although some lumbar veins may pass in front of them.
They lie on the bodies, medial to psoas.
The common iliac vessels lie behind the trunks at the pelvic brim

Last's says the common iliac vessels always lie in front of the trunks at the pelvic brim.
The trunks pass behind them into the pelvis.
Lumbar splanchnic nerves join the coeliac, aortic and superior hypogastric plexuses

Lumbar splanchnic nerves run medially to join the coeliac, aortic and superior hypogastric plexuses.
They supply the pelvic viscera through these plexuses.
Arise from S2, S3 and S4

The pelvic splanchnic nerves arise from S2, S3 and S4, the sacral parasympathetic outflow.
They are the nervi erigentes.
Are motor to the detrusor muscle

The pelvic splanchnic nerves are the main motor supply to the detrusor muscle.
So sacral cord lesions cause a flaccid bladder.
Supply the colon from the splenic flexure distally

Pelvic splanchnic fibres supply the colon from about the splenic flexure distally, some running up behind the peritoneum and some via the inferior mesenteric artery.
The vagus supplies the gut proximal to this.
Synapse in the inferior hypogastric plexus

Last's says none of the parasympathetic fibres synapse in the inferior hypogastric plexus; they relay in the walls of the viscera. About half the sympathetic fibres relay there.
Answer C: 1, 2 and 3.

questions.s: Concerning the sympathetic supply of the pelvic viscera:
o: It is motor to the internal urethral sphincter in the male

In the male, sympathetic fibres are motor to the internal urethral sphincter, preventing reflux of semen into the bladder during ejaculation.
Sympathectomy can cause retrograde ejaculation.
It is motor to the ductus deferens, seminal vesicles and prostate

Sympathetic fibres (L1, L2) are motor to the ductus deferens, seminal vesicles and prostate; emission is sympathetic.
Erection is parasympathetic.
Pain from the body of the uterus travels with the sympathetic nerves to T10 to L1

Pain from the body of the uterus travels with the sympathetic nerves to T10 to L1. Pain from the lower cervix travels with the parasympathetics.
This is why spinal anaesthesia must reach T10 for labour.
It carries the sensation of distension of the bladder

The sensation of bladder (and rectal) distension is carried by the pelvic splanchnic (parasympathetic) nerves.
The sympathetic fibres carry some pain from the bladder roof.

questions.s: After complete spinal cord transection above S2:
o: Afferent impulses of bladder distension cannot reach consciousness

Bladder distension afferents enter the cord at S2 to S4, so after a transection above S2 they cannot ascend to consciousness, although the sacral reflex can still empty the bladder.
The patient does not feel fullness.
The bladder may empty reflexly when distended

With the sacral centre intact, the bladder may empty reflexly when distended, as in the infant.
This is the "automatic" or reflex bladder.
Cortical inhibition of the sacral reflex is lost

Cortical inhibition of the sacral reflex, from the centre on the medial frontal surface, is lost after transection.
So the bladder empties without control.
The detrusor is permanently paralysed

Detrusor paralysis with overflow incontinence follows destruction of the sacral segments themselves (or their roots), not a transection above them.
Answer C: 1, 2 and 3.
Arises from S2, S3 and S4

The pudendal nerve arises from the anterior surfaces of the S2, S3 and S4 roots.
"S2, 3, 4 keeps the faeces off the floor."
Crosses the sacrospinous ligament medial to the pudendal vessels

The pudendal nerve crosses the sacrospinous ligament (near the ischial spine) medial to the pudendal vessels, briefly entering the gluteal region before entering the pudendal canal.
A pudendal block is aimed at the ischial spine.
Gives the inferior rectal nerve to the external anal sphincter

The pudendal nerve gives the inferior rectal nerve to the external anal sphincter. Its perineal branch supplies the external urethral sphincter.
Damage causes faecal and urinary incontinence.
Supplies the skin of the dorsum of the root of the penis

Last's says the dorsal nerve of the penis supplies the whole penis except the dorsum at its root, which is supplied by the ilioinguinal nerve (L1).
A pudendal block therefore spares the root.
The anal reflex depends on intact sacral segments

The anal reflex (pinprick of perianal skin causing contraction of the external sphincter) depends on intact sacral segments.
Its presence in cord injury suggests an incomplete lesion.
The bulbocavernosus reflex is mediated mainly by S3

Squeezing the glans contracts bulbospongiosus; this bulbocavernosus reflex depends on intact sacral segments, mainly S3.
Its return marks the end of spinal shock.
S4 supplies the perianal skin

S4 supplies the perianal skin; S5 and Co1 supply the skin behind the anus and over the coccyx.
The saddle area is S3 to S5.
Pain from the prostate may be referred to the posterior thigh

Last's says pain from the prostate may be referred, via the pelvic splanchnics (S2 to S4), to the posterior femoral cutaneous territory of the posterior thigh, mimicking sciatica.
All four true: E.
The greater splanchnic nerves pierce the crura to reach the coeliac ganglia

The greater (and lesser) splanchnic nerves pierce the crura of the diaphragm to reach the coeliac ganglia.
They carry preganglionic sympathetic fibres from T5 to T11.
Preganglionic fibres to the suprarenal medulla pass through without relay

Preganglionic sympathetic fibres to the suprarenal medulla pass through the coeliac plexus without relaying. Last's says the medulla is in effect a modified sympathetic ganglion.
Its cells are postganglionic neurons.
Its sympathetic fibres are excitatory to peristalsis

Sympathetic fibres of the coeliac plexus are inhibitory to peristalsis, motor to sphincters, vasomotor and sensory.
Parasympathetic fibres excite peristalsis.
The vagus contributes parasympathetic fibres to it

Vagal fibres (mainly from the posterior vagal trunk) enter the coeliac plexus and are distributed with its branches.
They pass through without synapse.
About 10% of its fibres are afferent

Last's says about 90 percent of the abdominal vagal fibres are afferent, serving reflex activity, not 10 percent.
The vagus is mainly a sensory nerve.
Highly selective vagotomy divides the branches to the pyloric antrum

Highly selective vagotomy divides only the branches to the fundus and body (acid-secreting parts), preserving the supply to the pyloric antrum (nerves of Latarjet).
So gastric emptying is preserved.
Vagal afferents carry the main pain sensation from the stomach

Pain from the abdominal viscera, including the stomach, runs with the sympathetic nerves. Vagal afferents carry reflex information and nausea.
So vagotomy does not abolish gastric pain.
Truncal vagotomy divides the trunks on the abdominal oesophagus

Truncal vagotomy divides both vagal trunks on the abdominal oesophagus, denervating the stomach and the other abdominal viscera.
Answer D: 4 only.
The medulla develops from neural crest

The suprarenal medulla develops from neural crest (chromaffin cells).
So it is related to sympathetic ganglia.
The cortex develops from the intermediate cell mass mesoderm

The suprarenal cortex is mesodermal, from the intermediate cell mass (coelomic epithelium).
Two different origins in one organ.
At birth the suprarenal is almost as large as the kidney

At birth the suprarenal is almost as large as the kidney, because of the large fetal cortex.
It shrinks rapidly after birth.
They receive both sympathetic and parasympathetic innervation

The suprarenals (and gonads) receive only sympathetic innervation.
There is no parasympathetic supply.
Connects the left branch of the portal vein to the inferior vena cava

The ductus venosus connects the left branch of the portal vein to the inferior vena cava, carrying blood from the left umbilical vein past the liver.
It shunts oxygenated blood to the heart.
Becomes the ligamentum venosum

After birth the ductus venosus becomes the ligamentum venosum, which lies in a fissure bounding the caudate lobe.
A useful landmark on the liver.
Is connected to the ligamentum teres

The ligamentum venosum is connected to the ligamentum teres (the obliterated left umbilical vein) at the left branch of the portal vein.
They form a continuous fibrous cord.
Closes at birth by muscular contraction triggered by oxygen

Closure by muscular contraction triggered by oxygen describes the ductus arteriosus. The ductus venosus clots off when flow stops.
Answer C: 1, 2 and 3.
The liver is relatively twice as large as in the adult

In the newborn the liver is relatively about twice as large as in the adult, and its lower border is palpable below the costal margin.
It occupies much of the abdomen.
The appendix arises from the apex of a conical caecum

In the newborn the caecum is conical and the appendix arises from its apex; later unequal growth of the caecal walls moves the base to the posteromedial wall.
This is the fetal type.
The fundus of the bladder lies above the symphysis pubis even when empty

In the newborn the fundus of the bladder lies above the symphysis pubis even when empty, because the pelvis is small.
The bladder is an abdominal organ in infants.
The kidneys have abundant perinephric fat

The newborn kidneys are lobulated and have very little perinephric fat.
So they are more mobile and easily felt.
The sacral plexus lies external to the parietal pelvic fascia

Last's principle: in the pelvis the nerves (sacral plexus) lie outside (external to) the parietal pelvic fascia, and the vessels lie inside it.
The plexus lies on piriformis behind the fascia.
Branches of the sacral plexus to the buttock pierce the parietal pelvic fascia

Last's says because the sacral plexus lies behind the fascia (between it and piriformis), its branches to the buttock do not need to pierce it.
Only the vessels have to pierce the fascia to leave.
The pudendal nerve leaves the pelvis above piriformis

The pudendal nerve leaves the pelvis below piriformis through the greater sciatic foramen, crosses the sacrospinous ligament and enters the pudendal canal through the lesser sciatic foramen.
Only the superior gluteal nerve and vessels pass above piriformis.
The internal iliac vessels lie external to the pelvic fascia

The internal iliac vessels lie inside (internal to) the parietal pelvic fascia.
Answer A: 1 only.
